attributes.body:
In Japanese, describing things that can be experienced with the senses (excluding visual), is a little bit different to the way that we would convey it in English. Traditionally, we would use unique verbs for each of these situations, such as 'smells like (A)', 'tastes like (A)', 'feels like (A)', etc. While this is still possible in Japanese, it is not the most common way.

がする is a grammar construction that focuses on the source of the smell, sound, taste, or feeling, and makes the sensory experience itself the subject of the sentence. To use がする, simply attach it to the end of any phrase that expresses which type of 'sense' is being created/given off by the subject.

Fun Fact

Japanese often uses 気（き） 'energy', 'spirit', as something that can be perceived with the senses. Due to this, there are many phrases which use ～気（き）がする in the same way as this grammar point.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: The extended use of する

attributes.body: がする and にみえる (often written in kanji as に見える) both describe sensations, but differ in usage. がする is used with sensory words, e.g. 音がする 'I hear', 匂いがする 'I smell', and 味がする 'I taste' (literally, 'It gives off a sound/smell/taste.'). に見える specifically describes visual sensations and means 'looks like', e.g. 石に見える ('It looks like a rock.'), without implying that it is the thing it visually resembles.

attributes.body: がする and 聞こえる both express sensory experiences, but differ in nuance.  がする is used with sensory words, e.g. 音がする 'I hear', 匂いがする 'I smell', and 味がする 'I taste' (literally, 'It gives off a sound/smell/taste.'). 聞こえる focuses specifically on sound and means 'to be heard' or 'to sound like', e.g. 音楽が聞こえる ('I hear music.') or 音楽に聞こえる ('It sounds like music.').
